Let d>1 be fixed. Choose any sufficiently large integer k and put n=k(k+1). Define
c=n^2,\qquad a=n^2+k^2,\qquad b=n^2+(k+1)^2.
They are distinct integers. Moreover,
\begin{aligned}
ab&=(n^2+k^2)(n^2+(k+1)^2)\\
&=n^4+n^2\bigl(k^2+(k+1)^2\bigr)+k^2(k+1)^2.
\end{aligned}
Since n^2=k^2(k+1)^2, division by c=n^2 gives
\[
\frac{ab}{c}=n^2+k^2+(k+1)^2+1\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Therefore c|ab.

The offsets of c,a,b from n^2 are respectively 0,k^2,(k+1)^2. Clearly k^2<n+d\sqrt n. Also,
\[
(k+1)^2\le n+d\sqrt n
\iff k+1\le d\sqrt{k(k+1)}.
\]
But
\[
\frac{k+1}{\sqrt{k(k+1)}}=\sqrt{1+\frac1k}\longrightarrow1<d,
\]
so the last inequality holds for all sufficiently large k. Consequently c,a,b all belong to [n^2,n^2+n+d\sqrt n]. Since infinitely many sufficiently large k give distinct n=k(k+1), the assertion follows.
